contributions.headingText: Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular neoplasm with endothelial differentiation.
2B56.Y & XH6264 Angiosarcoma, other specified primary site & Haemangiosarcoma
Not recommended: haemangiosarcoma; lymphangiosarcoma; malignant haemangioendothelioma; malignant angioendothelioma.

These tumours can arise in all compartments of the thorax (lungs, pleura, heart [see section Cardiac angiosarcoma], thymus, mediastinum) {20709359; 18987547}. They account for < 1% of mediastinal tumours {4331304; 13940960}, usually occurring in the anterior (prevascular) mediastinum. In children, the mediastinum is the most common site {18987547}. Pulmonary angiosarcomas arise from pulmonary vessels.
Symptoms/signs include chest pain, dyspnoea, cough, haemoptysis, pleural thickening, effusion, haemothorax, and cardiac compression {7974301; 21497371; 20709359}.
Thoracic angiosarcomas are more common in males. There is a wide age range, with peak incidence in the seventh decade of life. Angiosarcomas are rare in children {18987547; 1409148}.

For most cases, the etiology is unknown. A minority arise after radiation exposure {8756389}. Angiosarcoma has been associated with implanted foreign material, pre-existing haemangioma / vascular malformation, prior trauma/surgery, chronic tuberculous pyothorax, syndromes (e.g. neurofibromatosis and Maffucci syndrome), and rarely asbestos {12895234; 21497371; 3052791; 21659738; 10460655; 12360047; 20089367}.

Some harbour complex karyotypes {20217954; 25231439}. Angiogenesis genes and vascular-specific receptor tyrosine kinases (TIE1, TEK, KDR [VEGFR2], FLT4 [VEGFR3]) are frequently upregulated {19723655; 18041747}. A subset, typically younger patients, have CIC abnormalities {26735859}. Approximately 40% harbour recurrent somatic mutations involving angiogenic signalling pathways (in KDR, PTPRB, PLCG1), and rare mutations occur in RAS genes, PIK3CA, TP53, FLT4, and TIE1 {19723655; 22648906; 24633157}. MYC amplifications occur in almost all postradiation/lymphoedema-associated angiosarcomas {20949568; 20008140; 24329959; 22121953}.
Angiosarcoma is frequently infiltrative, ranging from haemorrhagic and spongy to solid and fleshy {9630175}.

Angiosarcomas range from anastomosing vessels to solid sheets of high-grade epithelioid or spindled cells with minimal vasoformation, often with mixtures of patterns. Vasoformative areas are lined by atypical endothelial cells, with frequent multilayering, hobnailing, or papillary-like projections. Epithelioid angiosarcomas typically have a sheet-like proliferation of cells with vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm, and only focal vasoformation {1718176}. Pleural angiosarcomas can mimic mesothelioma or carcinoma {10665909; 9181362}. Mitotic activity, necrosis, and haemorrhage are common. Pleural angiosarcomas are positive for CD31 and ERG, and variably positive for CD34 {7512718; 21317715; 11474291}. Keratin expression is sometimes seen with the epithelioid pattern {17284115; 1718176}. Radiation/lymphoedema-associated angiosarcomas are MYC-positive.
MYC amplification is present in radiation/lymphoedema-associated angiosarcomas {22121953; 21909081; 20949568}.

Essential:

  • Vasoformative to sheet-like
  • Endothelial cell multilayering
  • Nuclear atypia
  • Mitotic activity
  • CD31 and ERG positivity
Staging of angiosarcoma is not recommended, because the typically aggressive natural history of this tumour is not consistent with soft tissue staging systems.

These are aggressive neoplasms with a poor survival {29719795}. Anterior (prevascular) mediastinal angiosarcomas may have a more protracted course {20709359}.
